title: WITAWITADD - Empty Tombs
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ad5pxORFPfk

A short episode answering a recurring viewer complaint: in Dark Light Memento Mori, Warhammer Quest and now Advanced HeroQuest, whole stretches of the playthroughs go by where nothing happens. Daniel (@dungeondive) grants that it's a fair objection and then declines to share it.

His argument is that the nothing *is* the something. Moving through the dungeon, physically building it out of tiles, watching an unscripted layout take a shape no designer chose — that's the event. Unscripted dungeons often end up more evocative than scripted ones. He adds a little realism, unusually for someone who normally sides with Warren Spector on fun over realism: these tombs are centuries old and his party is not the first through the door. Maybe the last group took the final treasure. Maybe a roaming rat sprung the last trap. Empty rooms are what picked-over ruins look like, and the embellishment happens in his head even if he can't narrate purple prose on camera.

The comparison that anchors it is Dark Souls — Anor Londo's emptiness read as a deliberate choice, not a technical limit, and the source of its vastness. Set against that, he places over-scripted games like Sword & Sorcery and Middara, where every beat is somebody else's. Secrets of the Lost Tomb straddles both. And a live game of the 1979 module Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan — 'Boomer D&D,' per his DM — is supplying the quiet halls right now.

When everything is amped to eleven, he notes, nothing is.

----

Is an empty dungeon a design failure or part of the texture? And does your answer change when you're watching someone else play it rather than playing it yourself?
